_comment: Database statement semantics. ADR-0065. Issues tina4-python #133 and #138,
fixed at parity in all four frameworks.
Five rules, one fixture:
1. WRITE DETECTION. A statement is a write when, after string literals,
quoted identifiers and comments are scrubbed, its first word is INSERT,
UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, UPSERT or REPLACE, or it is a WITH whose body
holds a DML verb. When unsure, it is a write: a read misread as a write
only loses its pagination and cache for that one call.
2. FETCH OF A WRITE. fetch() / fetch_one() of a write runs it exactly once,
as written - no COUNT probe, no LIMIT / OFFSET / ROWS / TOP - is never
served from or stored in the query cache (it flushes the cache, like
execute()), and commits like execute() outside an explicit transaction.
3. EXECUTE RETURNS ROWS. execute() of a statement that produces rows
(SELECT, WITH ... SELECT, RETURNING, OUTPUT, CALL, EXEC) returns them in
the same result type fetch() returns. A plain write keeps the return
value it always had.
4. PLACEHOLDER TRANSLATION. Only a ? in SQL code is a placeholder. A ? inside
is text and is left alone.
5. NO PARAMETERS, NO REWRITE. SQL with no parameters is sent exactly as
written, so PostgreSQL's jsonb ?, ?| and ?& operators work. With
parameters, use jsonb_exists(), jsonb_exists_any(), jsonb_exists_all().
A literal % is doubled only for psycopg2 (Python) when parameters are
passed, because only there does the driver read every %.
THE VECTORS BELOW ARE DATA, NOT DOCUMENTATION. Each framework copies this
file byte-for-byte into its own test fixtures directory and its runner walks
write_detection_vectors and placeholder_vectors through the framework's own
function. A vector added here is a vector all four must answer identically.
The translation primitive differs by framework, so every runner maps the
placeholders to the SAME numbered form (:1, :2, ...) before comparing:
python  SQLTranslator.placeholder_style(sql, ':')
php     SQLTranslator::placeholderStyle($sql, ':')
ruby    Tina4::SQLTranslator.replace_placeholders(sql) { |i| ":#{i + 1}" }
nodejs  SQLTranslator.placeholderStyle(sql, ':')
The write detector is the one fetch() and the query cache already consult:
python  DatabaseAdapter._is_write_statement(sql)
php     Tina4\Database\SqlStatement::isWrite($sql)
ruby    Tina4::Database.write_statement?(sql)
nodejs  SQLTranslator.isWriteStatement(sql)
Behaviour cases run against REAL engines, no mocks: SQLite for fetch-of-write
and execute rows (every framework ships it), PostgreSQL for the
no-parameters rule, SQL Server for OUTPUT and EXEC. Durability is read back on
a SECOND, fresh connection, never on the connection that did the write.

write_detection_vectors.sql: UPDATE t SET a = 1 WHERE id = ?
MERGE INTO t USING s ON t.id = s.id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET a = s.a
INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (?) RETURNING id
WITH x AS (INSERT INTO t (a) VALUES (1) RETURNING id) SELECT id FROM x
WITH moved AS (DELETE FROM a RETURNING *) INSERT INTO b SELECT * FROM moved
WITH x AS (SELECT id FROM t) UPDATE t SET a = 1 WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM x)
select a from t where b = ?
WITH x AS (SELECT 1 AS n) SELECT n FROM x
WITH x AS (SELECT 'UPDATE' AS s) SELECT s FROM x

write_detection_vectors.note: known ceiling: only the SQL text is read, never a function body - wrap such a call in start_transaction() / commit()

placeholder_vectors.sql: SELECT * FROM t WHERE a = ? AND b = ?
placeholder_vectors.numbered: SELECT * FROM t WHERE a = :1 AND b = :2

placeholder_vectors.sql:
SELECT a -- why?
FROM t WHERE b = ?
placeholder_vectors.numbered:
SELECT a -- why?
FROM t WHERE b = :1

placeholder_vectors.sql: SELECT /* ? */ a FROM t WHERE b = ?
placeholder_vectors.numbered: SELECT /* ? */ a FROM t WHERE b = :1

placeholder_vectors.sql: SELECT a FROM t WHERE b LIKE 'x%' AND c = ?
placeholder_vectors.numbered: SELECT a FROM t WHERE b LIKE 'x%' AND c = :1

invariants.rule: The write detector answers every write_detection_vectors entry with its 'write' value. A write is a statement whose first word, after literals, quoted identifiers and comments are scrubbed and leading whitespace and parentheses are dropped, is INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, UPSERT or REPLACE, or a WITH whose scrubbed body contains INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or MERGE.
invariants.why: fetch(), fetch_one() and the query cache all branch on this one answer. Four detectors that disagree on a single statement give four different commit, pagination and cache behaviours for the same SQL.
cases: write detection answers every fixture vector

invariants.rule: fetch() and fetch_one() of INSERT ... RETURNING run the statement exactly once (one row lands), with no COUNT probe and no LIMIT / OFFSET appended, and commit it outside an explicit transaction, so a second, fresh connection sees the row. With the query cache on, the same fetched write run twice inserts two rows and a cached read taken before it is flushed.
invariants.why: Issue #133: fetch() wrapped a write in a COUNT probe and a LIMIT, ran it twice on some engines, never committed it on others, and could hand back a cached id for a row that did not exist. The caller got an id for a row no other connection could see.
cases: fetch of an insert returning runs once and commits
fetch one of an insert returning runs once and commits
a fetched write is never cached and flushes the cache

invariants.rule: execute() of SELECT, WITH ... SELECT and INSERT ... RETURNING returns the same result type fetch() returns, carrying the rows. On SQL Server, execute() of INSERT ... OUTPUT inserted.id and of EXEC of a procedure that selects rows returns those rows. execute() of a plain INSERT with no RETURNING keeps the framework's existing plain-write return value.
invariants.why: execute() used to return a bare success flag for a row-producing statement on some adapters, so the RETURNING id was silently thrown away and a SELECT through execute() answered 'true'.
cases: execute returns rows for select with select and returning
execute of a plain write keeps its return value
execute returns rows for output and exec on sql server

invariants.rule: Numbered placeholder translation answers every placeholder_vectors entry with its 'numbered' value: a ? inside '...', E'...' (backslash escapes), $$...$$, $tag$...$tag$, "...", `...`, -- comments and /* */ comments is left alone, and a literal % is never touched by the numbered form.
invariants.why: Issue #138: translation was a plain text replace, so SELECT 'why?', ? gained a second placeholder and failed with an index error, and a ? in a comment or identifier shifted every later parameter by one.
cases: placeholder translation answers every fixture vector

invariants.rule: Against a real PostgreSQL: fetch() with no parameters of SELECT '{"a":1}'::jsonb ? 'a', ?| array['a','z'] and ?& array['a'] returns true for all three, and SELECT 'a%' returns the two characters a%. With parameters, jsonb_exists('{"a":1}'::jsonb, ?) with ['a'] returns true and SELECT 'a%' || ? with ['b'] returns a%b.
invariants.why: Issue #138 follow-up: SQL with no parameters was still run through the ? translator (turning jsonb ? into a placeholder) and through psycopg2's % doubling (turning a% into a%%). No parameters means nothing to bind, so nothing may be rewritten.
cases: sql with no parameters is sent exactly as written on postgresql
jsonb exists functions and literal percent work with parameters on postgresql
